title: APT, Message, Image, Attachment, and Browser Vectors

blocks.text: A **vector** is the path by which a threat reaches its target. Objective 2.3 requires recognizing fifteen vector families. Let's start with those that pass through communication and the workstation.

blocks.field: Targeted, long-term campaign conducted by an organized, well-funded actor that combines multiple vectors and pursues a strategic objective rather than immediate gain.

blocks.note: Targeted attacks and persistent threats (printed pp. 6-7)

blocks.text: An APT is not malware: it is a **campaign**. It is defined by persistence, targeting, and resources, not by a single tool.

head: Vector
Concrete Example
Watchpoint
rows: Email
Phishing with attachment or link to a fake portal
Spoofed sender, lookalike domain (typosquatting)
SMS
Smishing: link to a fake bank site
Shortened link hides the real domain
Instant messaging / collaboration tools
Direct message in Teams or Slack with a malicious link
Trust in the internal channel lowers vigilance

blocks.field: Successor to SMS in mobile messaging. Vector for phishing via rich messages, attachments, and links, difficult to filter with traditional email controls.

blocks.text: **RCS** is listed in §2.3 of the objectives; none of the four books covers it. Remember it as a mobile variant of message-based phishing.

items: **QR codes / quishing**: scanning a code opens a fake payment or login site — the QR code hides the URL, neutralizing human inspection.
**Embedded content**: active content hidden inside an apparently harmless image or document.
**CAPTCHA**: fake "I am not a robot" check that masks a download or redirects to a booby-trapped site.
**Embedded macros**: Office macro executed when opening a document, often after clicking "Enable Content".
**RTF and PDF**: formats capable of embedding objects, scripts, or links exploiting an unpatched reader.

blocks.note: Official objectives — QR codes / quishing, RCS, and embedded content absent from the 4 books

blocks.text: Quishing, QR codes, malicious embedded content, and deepfakes are vectors **required by the objectives** but not covered by the provided books. The definitions above come from the objectives and industry practice.

head: Element
Risk
rows: Browser extensions
A compromised extension reads pages, cookies, and sessions.
JavaScript
Hostile script on a page or via an ad (malvertising).
Password managers
Vault targeted by phishing or a malicious extension; the master password becomes a single point of failure.
Cookies / session tokens
Session hijacking: the attacker takes over a valid session without password or MFA.

blocks.q: A user scans a QR code on a poster and enters their credentials on a convincing fake login page. Which vector?
blocks.explain: A QR code is classified as an image-based vector; quishing is its phishing variant.

items: An APT is a durable, targeted campaign, not simple malware.
Message: email, SMS, RCS, instant messaging, collaboration tools.
Image and attachment: QR/quishing, embedded content, CAPTCHA, macros, RTF, PDF.
Browser: extensions, JavaScript, password managers, cookies, and session tokens.

title: Network, Remote Access, Endpoint, Supply Chain, and Signal Vectors

blocks.text: The remaining vectors no longer go through the user: they exploit infrastructure, devices, trusted third parties, or radio waves. Here the exam tests the distinction between **network, endpoint, human, IoT, OT, and signals**.

head: Vector
Example
rows: Network-based
Compromised router, switch, firewall, or virtualized appliance; session key theft.
Remote access
Exposed RDP, VNC without strong authentication, VPN with stolen credentials.

blocks.chapter: Select and Collect the Right Data
blocks.note: Network visibility and infrastructure vectors (printed p. 204)

items: **Mobile devices / tablets / workstations / servers**: each device type has its own vectors (mobile app, firmware, exposed service).
**Trusted devices**: an already-trusted device is an effective vector because it bypasses perimeter detection.
**Built-in tools / living-off-the-land**: PowerShell, WMI, certutil, or cmd used to execute without dropping a binary — hence the importance of behavioral telemetry.

blocks.text: The **supply chain** vector goes through a trusted third party: software vendor, MSP, logistics provider, or SaaS. A malicious software update is more dangerous than a direct attack because it is signed and distributed through the legitimate channel. External media (malicious USB) remains a major physical vector.

blocks.note: Third-party dependencies, vendors, and supply chain (printed pp. 231-233)

blocks.text: Human Factor, IoT, OT, and Physical

blocks.note: Social engineering, impersonation, and visitors (printed pp. 37-42)

head: Vector
Example
rows: Human-based
Impersonation, contractor, visitor, spoofed biometrics, watering hole.
IoT-based
Compromised camera, sensor, or printer serving as an entry point.
OT-based
Operational network / SCADA: industrial controllers and systems.
Physical-based
Lock and key, access mantrap, badges: bypass via tailgating or lost badge.

blocks.note: OT / SCADA and network equipment (printed p. 123)

blocks.field: Exploitation of short-range wireless communications: Bluetooth (hostile pairing, bluebugging), radio frequency (interception or injection), and NFC (proximity read/write, payment or badge).

blocks.note: Official objectives — none of the 4 books covers Bluetooth / RF / NFC as vectors

blocks.text: Bluetooth, radio frequency, and NFC are **required in §2.3** but absent from the provided books. Remember the logic: proximity + wireless channel + device trust = vector.
An NFC badge read by a hostile phone, a compromised IoT printer, and an MSP suffering a breach are three different vectors: **signal**, **IoT**, and **supply chain**.

blocks.q: A provider hosting your email is compromised and its admin credentials are used against you. Which vector?
blocks.explain: The trusted third party (SaaS/MSP) is the supply chain-based vector, even if the attacker subsequently uses credentials.

items: Network: infrastructure, virtualized devices, session keys; remote access: RDP, VNC, VPN.
Endpoint: trusted devices and built-in tools (living-off-the-land).
Supply chain: vendors, MSPs, logistics, SaaS; external media: malicious USB.
Human, IoT, OT, physical, and signals (Bluetooth/RF/NFC — gap relative to the books).
